newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Focus-Tietmeyer sees end to Buba-Bonn gold crisis.
newsitem.headline: Focus-Tietmeyer sees end to Buba-Bonn gold crisis.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer on Wednesday heralded an end to the bitter strife between the hardline Bundesbank and the cash-strapped Bonn government over plans to revalue assets.

Tietmeyer said he had received reassuring messages from Finance Minister Theo Waigel that he would not be forced into a revaluation process that would end up easing Germany's path to monetary union by yielding a windfall profit for Bonn in 1997.

"I have the impression that we can find a solution," he said, addressing reporters after attending a session with other top central bankers at the International Monetary Conference in Interlaken, Switzerland.

Tietmeyer made clear that he firmly objected to Bonn's original plan to start revaluing gold and currency reserves nearer to their market value this year, and transferring the resultant profit immediately to state coffers to help it plug its gaping deficit in 1997.

The new plans under discussion in Bonn would delay the transfer process until 1998, thus eliminating any impact on Germany's budget position for 1997. This year is crucial for economic and monetary union (EMU), since the choice of participants will be made on the basis of 1997 figures
"To meet the (EMU) criteria via creating money is not the best solution," Tietmeyer said.
"Thus we have made clear that it would not be appropriate to deliver more profit this year."
He added that it remained to be seen whether this process would require any changes to Bundesbank statutes.
The fight over reserve revaluations reared up last week, when the Bundesbank issued a statement flatly rejecting Waigel's revaluation proposal.

While not in principle opposed to revaluing reserves, the Bundesbank viewed the timing of the proposal as a threat to Germany's image as a by-the-rules player on monetary union and to the bank's own independence.
"We have always said that revaluation of some assets seems to be appropriate as the risks have changed and will change," Tietmeyer said.
"We are willing to do so (revalue) but we say it is not appropriate to do that mid-year and to do that for a special purpose to finance the present budget," he added.
Along with currency reserves, the Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold, valued at 13.7 billion marks compared to a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.
It was not immediately clear on Wednesday which kind of reserves were affected by the revised revaluation plan.
Germany is struggling in particular to plug its budget deficit, with the Maastricht Treaty calling for countries to limit their deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
Tietmeyer also made clear that Bonn and the Bundesbank were absolutely in agreement on the idea that there should be no sales of gold.
He also said he hoped that monetary union could still go ahead on schedule, amid "appropriate fulfilment of the convergence criteria."

Waigel and Tietmeyer had met on Tuesday to strike a compromise on Bonn's plans to revalue the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves, thus easing a dispute that has triggered calls for Waigel to resign.
Confusion resulted as the Finance Minister and Bundesbank chief appeared to leave the meeting with divergent understandings of what went on.
Waigel had declared a compromise was reached, while Tietmeyer, arriving in Interlaken on Tuesday night, said talks had been held but "no deal" had resulted.
Tietmeyer repeated on Wednesday that there had been no formal agreement with Bonn.
Waigel also issued a clarifying statement on Wednesday that was agreed with the Bundesbank.

The statement said he and Tietmeyer had held talks on the revaluation issue, that there would be a serious attempt to agree to revalue certain assets in 1997 but delay the transfer of profit until 1998, and that more legal questions needed to be discussed.
